entries.label: Primary resources assumed to be the quick and cheap option
entries.description: Reverses the trade-off: field data is accurate but costly; secondary data is cheap but second-hand.
entries.signal: The answer attributes low cost or speed to primary collection.

refutation.text_md: There is a real trade-off here, and you are reaching for it.
It runs the other way: PRIMARY resources are the accurate ones and cost the most time, effort and money. SECONDARY resources save all three but you did not control how they were gathered.

entries.label: Ready-made data called a primary resource
entries.description: Classifies data taken from published records as field data because the student gathered it themselves.
entries.signal: A record, website or publication is described as a primary resource.

refutation.text_md: Collecting the data yourself does feel like field work — that is the honest confusion here.
What decides it is where the data ORIGINATED. Figures already compiled by someone else are SECONDARY, however you obtained them.
Primary means you generated the observations: a questionnaire you distributed, an interview you conducted, a count you made.

entries.label: A sample assumed to be more accurate than a census
entries.description: Justifies sampling by accuracy rather than by cost, size or destructive testing.
entries.signal: The reason given for sampling is that it is more accurate.

refutation.text_md: Sampling is the right method in that situation — the reason is what slipped.
A census covers every value, so it is the MORE accurate method. We sample when a census is impossible or self-defeating: the society is gigantic, or the test destroys what it measures.
Testing every lamp until it burns out would leave nothing to sell.

entries.label: Equal means, so equally spread
entries.description: The student finds that two sets have the same mean and concludes that their values are equally spread out, or that the sets are alike.
entries.signal: Says two sets with the same mean have the same dispersion, without finding either range.

refutation.text_md: You found that both means are equal, and that part is right: both sets of wages have a mean of LE 200. The slip is in treating the mean as if it also told you how spread out the values are.
Look at the two sets of wages. Set A is $170, 180, 180, 230, 240$ and set B is $50, 180, 180, 190, 400$. Both add up to $1000$, so both have mean $200$.

But the values are not equally spread. Set A stays between $170$ and $240$, close to its mean. Set B runs from $50$ up to $400$, far on both sides of $200$. The mean is the same, yet B is clearly more scattered.
The mean tells you where the centre of the values is. It says nothing about how far the values stretch around that centre. Sets with the same mean can have very different spreads.
To compare dispersion, find the range of each set as greatest value $-$ smallest value. Compare the two ranges: the bigger range means the more divergent set.

verdict.reason: Uses the book's wage sets (both mean 200, sums 1000 correct). Describes the spread correctly (A 170-240, B 50-400). Range method matches the canonical solution, and the bigger-range-means-more-divergent conclusion matches it too. It argues against this specific error. Remark rule-7 and the canonical items support it.

entries.label: Squared deviations summed but not averaged
entries.description: Divides by nothing before taking the root, so the sum is used in place of its mean.

refutation.text_md: Your deviations and their squares are right.
They have to be AVERAGED before the root: divide the sum by $n$, the number of values.
Sum $= 8$, $n = 4$, so the average is $2$ and $\sigma = \sqrt{2}$ — not $\sqrt{8}$.
The formula carries the division inside the root: $\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (x - \bar{x})^2}{n}}$.

verdict.reason: Omitting the division by n is a plausible slip against the canonical formula σ=√(Σ(x−x̄)²/n). The refutation's arithmetic is correct: 3,5,5,7 has mean 5, squared deviations sum to 8, n=4, so σ=√2. It uses the book's method, names no outside references, and contrasts √8 with √2.
